articles.label: Government
articles.headline: Escambia County's $47 Million Stormwater Problem Has No Fix in Sight
articles.dek: Three years after voters approved a dedicated fee, the county has spent more on consultants than actual drainage improvements. Records show why.
brief: Escambia County has collected $47.2 million in stormwater fees since 2023 but completed only 12 of 89 planned drainage projects
Public records show $8.3 million paid to engineering consultants while actual construction spending totaled $6.1 million
County staff blame permitting delays and rising costs, but emails reveal repeated warnings about administrative bottlenecks went unaddressed
articles.body:
The water pooled in Doris Harmon's front yard for eleven days last September. It crept up to her doorstep, killed her azaleas, and left a tideline of mud on her brick foundation. She lives on Dorado Drive in the Myrtle Grove area, one of 23 streets the county identified in 2022 as critical flood zones requiring immediate drainage improvements.

Three years later, the project hasn't broken ground.

"They told us help was coming," Harmon said. "I voted for that fee. I've paid it every month. Where did the money go?"

The Flightline reviewed more than 1,400 pages of county records, contracts, and internal emails obtained through public records requests. The documents reveal a stormwater program that collected $47.2 million from property owners between November 2023 and May 2026 but completed just 12 of 89 planned projects. Meanwhile, spending on engineering consultants and studies exceeded actual construction costs by more than $2 million.

The Promise

Escambia County voters approved the stormwater utility fee in August 2022 by a margin of 58% to 42%. The campaign was straightforward: recurring floods were damaging homes and roads, federal grants required local matching funds, and the county needed a dedicated revenue stream to fix aging drainage infrastructure.

County Administrator Wes Moreno told commissioners at the time that the fee would fund "shovel-ready projects within 18 months." He presented a list of 89 priority sites, ranked by flood frequency and property damage estimates. The Myrtle Grove neighborhood alone had seven streets on the list.

The fee took effect in November 2023. A single-family homeowner pays $7.50 per month, or $90 annually. Commercial properties pay based on impervious surface area. The county projected $15 million to $17 million in annual revenue.

That projection proved accurate. Collections hit $15.8 million in fiscal 2024 and $16.9 million in fiscal 2025. Through May 2026, the current fiscal year has brought in $14.5 million.

The money arrived. The drainage work did not.

Where the Money Went

The county's stormwater fund expenditure reports, obtained through a June 2026 public records request, show how the $47.2 million was allocated:

Engineering and consulting services: $8.3 million. This includes contracts with three firms—CDM Smith, Atkins North America, and a local firm called Baskerville-Donovan—for project design, environmental assessments, and program management.

Construction: $6.1 million across 12 completed projects and three ongoing ones. The largest completed project was a $1.9 million culvert replacement on Navy Boulevard. Most others were drainage ditch cleanings and pipe repairs costing between $80,000 and $400,000 each.

Personnel: $4.2 million for salaries and benefits. The county created a stormwater division in 2024 with 14 full-time positions, though records show only nine were filled as of April 2026.

Equipment and vehicles: $1.8 million.

Debt service: $3.1 million. The county issued bonds in 2024 anticipating future fee revenue.

Administrative overhead: $2.4 million for office costs, software, and interdepartmental charges.

The remaining $21.3 million sits in reserve accounts. County budget documents describe this as "encumbered for future project phases," but no construction contracts have been executed for those funds.

The Consultant Question

The $8.3 million in consulting fees drew the sharpest questions at a June 2026 commission meeting.

"We're paying people to study the problem more than we're paying people to fix it," said District 4 Commissioner Robert Bender. "That's backwards."

County Public Works Director Marcus Franklin defended the spending. Design work must precede construction, he said. Environmental permits require detailed engineering plans. Federal grant applications demand certified studies.

"You can't build something you haven't designed," Franklin told commissioners. "These are sequential steps."

But internal emails from 2024 and 2025 suggest the sequencing was not the only problem.

In March 2024, a project manager at CDM Smith emailed Franklin's deputy to flag delays in county reviews. "We submitted the 60% design documents on January 15," the email reads. "It is now March 22 and we have received no comments. Our team cannot proceed to final design without county approval at this stage."

The deputy's response, sent four days later: "Still working through the queue. We are short-staffed."

Similar exchanges appear throughout the records. A September 2024 email from Baskerville-Donovan notes that permit applications for three Myrtle Grove projects had been "pending county signature" for 11 weeks. An October 2024 memo from the county's environmental compliance office warned that two projects faced permit expiration if construction didn't begin by March 2025. Neither did.

When asked about the staffing shortages, Franklin said the county struggled to compete with private-sector salaries. "We've had positions posted for over a year," he said. "The engineering market in this region is tight."

The Federal Delay

County officials also point to federal permitting as a bottleneck. Four of the largest planned projects involve work in or near wetlands, requiring U.S. Army Corps of Engineers approval under Section 404 of the Clean Water Act.

Franklin said the Corps has a backlog of permit applications stretching 18 to 24 months in the Mobile District, which covers Northwest Florida.

A Corps spokesperson confirmed the backlog but declined to comment on specific Escambia County projects, citing pending applications.

The county's records show it submitted Corps permit applications for two projects in August 2024. Neither has been approved. The other two wetland-adjacent projects haven't yet reached the federal permitting stage because county-level design reviews remain incomplete.

Rising Costs

The numbers from 2022 no longer hold.

When commissioners approved the priority project list, the county estimated total construction costs at $78 million over 10 years. Updated estimates from March 2026 put the figure at $112 million—a 44% increase.

Materials costs drove much of the jump. PVC pipe prices rose 31% between 2022 and 2025, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics producer price index. Concrete increased 22%. Labor costs in the Pensacola construction market climbed 18% over the same period, per data from the Florida Department of Economic Opportunity.

The county's original timeline assumed completing all 89 projects by 2032. Current projections show 34 projects completed by that date if funding and pace remain constant. The remaining 55 would stretch into the late 2030s.

"We're honest about it—we're behind," Franklin said. "But we're building a program from scratch. That takes time."

What Residents See

Dorado Drive still floods. So does Twin Oak Drive, West Yonge Street, and most of the other streets that appeared on the 2022 priority list.

At a neighborhood association meeting in June, Myrtle Grove residents pressed County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes the area. Why were they still waiting? When would construction begin?

Bergosh said he shared their frustration. He blamed county staff for moving too slowly and promised to push for faster action.

"I've been beating this drum for two years," Bergosh said. "Something has to change."

He did not specify what.

In the parking lot afterward, Doris Harmon said she'd stopped expecting answers. She's priced out sandbags. She's looking into flood insurance, though her street isn't in a FEMA-designated flood zone and private coverage would cost $2,400 annually.

"I'm 71 years old," she said. "I just want to stay in my house. But every time it rains hard, I can't sleep."

The stormwater fee shows up on her utility bill each month. She pays it. The water still comes.

This article is based on county expenditure reports, contract documents, meeting minutes, and internal emails obtained through public records requests filed in May and June 2026. The Flightline requested an interview with County Administrator Wes Moreno. A spokesperson said Moreno was unavailable but provided a written statement affirming the county's commitment to the stormwater program.

articles.label: Housing
articles.headline: The Last Mobile Home Park on Pensacola Beach
articles.dek: Residents of Via de Luna's Camp Gulf have watched the island transform around them for decades. Now the landowner wants to sell, and 23 families are running out of time.
brief: Camp Gulf, the last mobile home park on Pensacola Beach, faces closure after landowner files preliminary paperwork with Santa Rosa County for a zoning change
23 families, some who have lived there for over 30 years, have until December 31 to relocate under current lease terms
The 4.2-acre parcel on Via de Luna is assessed at $8.7 million and has drawn interest from at least two hotel developers
articles.body:
The wind comes off the Gulf around 4 p.m. most summer days, and when it does, Linda Haworth opens every window in her single-wide. She has lived in Lot 17 at Camp Gulf for 31 years. She knows the rhythms of this barrier island better than most of the tourists who drive past her home on their way to the Portofino towers.

"They don't even see us," Haworth said. "We're behind the palm trees. We're not part of the postcard."

For now, Camp Gulf exists in a kind of geographic paradox—4.2 acres of working-class Florida tucked between a $400-per-night vacation rental complex and a waterfront lot where a Miami-based developer recently broke ground on luxury condominiums. The mobile home park predates the Pensacola Beach we know today, the one with the Margaritaville sign and the spring break reputation. It has survived four hurricanes, two economic collapses, and decades of pressure to sell.

That pressure has finally won.

The Letter

In April, residents received a letter from Coastal Holdings LLC, the entity that has owned the land beneath their homes since 1987. The letter informed them that Coastal Holdings had entered into a purchase agreement with an unnamed buyer and would not be renewing ground leases when they expire December 31, 2026.

The letter was two paragraphs. It thanked residents for their "years of tenancy."

"Thirty-one years," Haworth said. "Two paragraphs."

Camp Gulf operates like most mobile home parks in Florida—residents own their manufactured homes but lease the land beneath them. Monthly lot rent runs $875, a figure that has increased roughly 4% annually for the past decade. That's still a fraction of what even a modest apartment costs on the beach. A one-bedroom at the Gulf Breeze complex a half-mile east lists at $2,400.

The math explains why people stay. It doesn't capture why leaving feels like something closer to exile.

Who Lives Here

The 23 occupied lots at Camp Gulf house a population that doesn't fit the Pensacola Beach brochure. There's a retired Navy cook who moved here in 1994 and never left. A single mother who works the front desk at a beach hotel and walks to her shift. A commercial fisherman who keeps his boat at the Sabine Marina and has lived at Camp Gulf longer than any current resident—38 years come October.

His name is Dale Hutchins. He's 71. He doesn't want to talk about the future.

"I've said my piece to whoever would listen," Hutchins said, standing in the crushed-shell parking area outside his double-wide. "None of it mattered."

Hutchins attended the Santa Rosa County Commission meeting in May when Coastal Holdings' attorney presented a preliminary application to rezone the parcel from residential to commercial-tourist. The rezoning would allow for hotel construction up to 75 feet—the current limit for most of the beach's commercial corridor.

The commission took no action. The application is still listed as "pending initial review" on the county's development portal.

What Comes Next

Santa Rosa County property records show the Camp Gulf parcel assessed at $8.7 million, a figure that reflects land value only. The manufactured homes belong to residents. Under Florida law, they'll have to move them or sell them—likely at a loss—when the leases expire.

Moving a single-wide costs between $8,000 and $15,000, according to estimates from two Pensacola-area mobile home transport companies. A double-wide can run $20,000 or more. And that's assuming you have somewhere to take it.

The closest mobile home parks accepting new residents are in Perdido Key—about 20 miles west—and Pace, roughly 25 miles north. Neither is on the water. Neither is walking distance to work.

"They keep saying there's an affordable housing crisis," said Maria Santos, who has lived at Camp Gulf for eight years with her two teenage daughters. "Then they do this. Where's the crisis they're solving?"

Santos works as a housekeeper at the Holiday Inn Express on Via de Luna, a seven-minute walk from her front door. She doesn't own a car. Her daughters attend Gulf Breeze High School and take the bus from the beach every morning.

"We're not asking for charity," Santos said. "We pay our rent. We've always paid our rent."

The Island's Memory

Pensacola Beach wasn't always a place for timeshares and tiki bars. Before the first high-rise went up in the 1980s, the island had a scrappier character—fish camps, beach shacks, seasonal workers who made the tourist economy run.

Camp Gulf is the last physical evidence of that era. The land it sits on is leased from the Santa Rosa Island Authority, which holds all beach property in trust for the public. SRIA granted a 99-year sublease to a private developer in 1954. That lease transfers to whoever buys the parcel now.

SRIA Executive Director Paolo Ghio confirmed the authority has been "in communication" with Coastal Holdings about the pending sale but declined to discuss specifics.

"The lease terms allow for commercial development consistent with the area's zoning," Ghio said. "Our role is administrative."

County Commissioner Dave Piech, whose district includes Pensacola Beach, said he's heard from Camp Gulf residents but has limited authority over private land transactions.

"I understand the hardship," Piech said. "But the county can't force a private landowner to continue operating a mobile home park."

He paused.

"I wish I had a better answer."

What Gets Lost

On a Tuesday evening in early July, Linda Haworth sat on her porch and watched the sunset light turn the Gulf the color of a bruised peach. She's lived through Ivan in 2004, through the oil spill in 2010, through the slow creep of development that has transformed the beach from a quirky Florida outpost into something that looks increasingly like everywhere else.

Her home is paid off. Her lot rent is current through the end of the year. After that, she doesn't know.

"My son keeps saying I should come live with him in Tennessee," Haworth said. "He's got a spare room."

She looked out at the water.

"I'm 67 years old. I've lived on this island for most of my adult life. What do you do with that? Put it in a box and take it to Tennessee?"

There's no good answer to that question. The economics of the situation are clear. The land beneath Camp Gulf is worth more as a hotel than as a place where 23 families live. That's how markets work. That's how barrier islands work, eventually.

But something disappears when the last affordable housing leaves a place. The people who clean the hotel rooms and cook the restaurant food and run the charter boats—they have to live somewhere. And when somewhere becomes nowhere, the island loses something that doesn't show up on a property assessment.

Dale Hutchins has watched Pensacola Beach change for nearly four decades. He's seen the dunes get bigger after each hurricane, seen the condo towers rise, seen the day-trippers replaced by Airbnb guests who never learn anyone's name.

"The beach doesn't remember," Hutchins said. "That's what people don't understand. The sand shifts. The buildings go up. And nobody remembers who was here before."

He's not asking for sympathy. He's stating a fact.

The Camp Gulf residents have until December 31 to find new homes. The rezoning application is pending. The unnamed buyer is waiting. And the wind still comes off the Gulf around 4 p.m. most summer days, whether anyone is there to open the windows or not.

articles.label: Military
articles.headline: Blue Angels 2027 Season in Doubt as Navy Weighs Super Hornet Transition Timeline
articles.dek: Internal documents suggest the team may need to pause operations during the switch from F/A-18 Hornets. Pensacola tourism officials are already nervous.
brief: Navy planning documents indicate the Blue Angels may suspend air show operations for 6-12 months during the transition from legacy Hornets to Super Hornets
Pensacola tourism officials estimate a full-season pause could cost the local economy $40-50 million in lost visitor spending
The transition timeline remains fluid, with final decisions expected by late 2026
articles.body:
The diamond formation roared over Pensacola Beach last March, six blue-and-gold jets trailing white smoke against a cloudless sky. Thirty thousand people crammed the sand to watch. By 2027, that crowd might be staring at an empty horizon.

Internal Navy planning documents obtained by The Flightline suggest the Blue Angels demonstration squadron could suspend air show operations for up to a year as the team transitions from its aging F/A-18 Hornets to the larger, more powerful F/A-18 Super Hornets. The documents, dated April 2026 and marked "pre-decisional," outline multiple scenarios ranging from a compressed three-month conversion to a full 12-month operational pause.

"Nothing is finalized," said Lt. Cmdr. Brian Hayes, a spokesman for Naval Air Forces. "The transition planning process is ongoing and involves multiple stakeholders. We're committed to minimizing any disruption to our air show schedule."

Hayes declined to confirm the authenticity of the documents or comment on specific timelines.

The Clock on the Legacy Hornets

The Blue Angels have flown the F/A-18 Hornet since 1986. The aircraft the team currently operates are among the oldest in Navy inventory, with some airframes approaching 10,000 flight hours. The Navy announced in 2020 that the team would eventually transition to Super Hornets—the same aircraft flown by the fleet—but has repeatedly declined to set a firm date.

The Super Hornet is 25 percent larger than the legacy Hornet, with more powerful engines and different flight characteristics. Pilots will need extensive retraining. Ground crews will need to learn new maintenance procedures. The team's signature maneuvers may need to be redesigned to account for the aircraft's different performance envelope.

"You can't just swap the jets and fly the same show," said retired Navy Cmdr. Frank Weisser, who flew with the Blue Angels from 2008 to 2010. "Every formation, every timing, every sight picture the pilots use—all of that changes. It's essentially building a new demonstration from scratch."

Weisser, who now works as an aviation consultant in Virginia Beach, said a six-month transition would be "aggressive but doable" while anything shorter would be "unrealistic."

Tourism Officials Watch Nervously

The Blue Angels fly approximately 60 air shows per year across North America. But Pensacola holds a special claim. The team has been based at Naval Air Station Pensacola since 1949. The annual homecoming show each November anchors the region's tourism calendar.

Visit Pensacola, the county's tourism marketing arm, estimates Blue Angels-related tourism generates between $80 and $100 million annually for Escambia County. That figure includes the homecoming show, weekly practice sessions that draw hundreds of spectators to viewing areas, and general brand awareness that links Pensacola to the iconic squadron.

"The Blue Angels are Pensacola," said Darien Schaefer, president and CEO of Visit Pensacola. "When people think of this city, they think of the Blue Angels. A pause in operations would be felt across every sector of our hospitality industry."

Schaefer said his office has been in contact with Navy officials but has received no definitive information about 2027 scheduling. He estimated a full-season pause could cost the local economy $40 to $50 million in lost visitor spending.

"We're planning for multiple scenarios," Schaefer said. "But there's no replacing the Blue Angels. There's no substitute attraction we can just plug in."

Hotel Owners Already Asking Questions

At the Hampton Inn on Pensacola Beach, general manager Teresa Morales said she started fielding calls from corporate headquarters in June asking about 2027 projections. The hotel typically books solid for homecoming weekend by August of the prior year. Rates can exceed $300 per night.

"We haven't seen the normal early booking pattern," Morales said. "People are waiting. They're hearing rumors. They want to know if the show is happening before they commit."

Similar uncertainty ripples through the restaurant and retail sectors. Flounder's Chowder House on Pensacola Beach reported that homecoming weekend 2025 was its highest-grossing weekend of the year, surpassing even the July Fourth holiday.

"You get people from all over the country," said assistant manager David Chen. "Families, veterans, aviation buffs. They come specifically for this. If it doesn't happen, they don't come."

The Broader Navy Calculus

The transition decision involves factors well beyond Pensacola's economic concerns. The Navy is managing a fleet-wide aircraft shortage, with operational squadrons competing for Super Hornets. The Blue Angels, while high-profile, are not a combat unit. In resource allocation discussions, demonstration teams typically rank below deployable squadrons.

The planning documents obtained by The Flightline reference "aircraft availability constraints" and "fleet prioritization requirements" as factors in the transition timeline. One scenario describes a phased approach where the Blue Angels would receive aircraft only after specific fleet squadrons complete their own transitions.

Retired Rear Adm. Peter Fanta, who served as director of surface warfare from 2014 to 2016, said the Navy faces legitimate competing pressures.

"The Blue Angels are important for recruiting, for public relations, for maintaining that connection between the Navy and the American people," Fanta said. "But if you're the fleet commander and you're short on Super Hornets for your carriers, you're not going to prioritize a demonstration team. The math doesn't work that way."

What Happens Next

Navy officials indicated a final decision on the transition timeline is expected by late 2026, likely after the conclusion of this year's air show season in November. That would give tourism officials and hospitality businesses roughly four months to prepare for whatever 2027 holds.

Some in Pensacola are already thinking about contingencies. Escambia County Commissioner Jeff Bergosh floated the idea at a June board meeting of organizing an alternative aviation event if the Blue Angels are unavailable.

"We can't control what the Navy decides," Bergosh said. "But we can start thinking about how to keep people coming here regardless. Maybe that's a vintage aircraft show, maybe that's something else. We need to be proactive."

For now, the Blue Angels continue their regular practice schedule at NAS Pensacola. The familiar roar of six jets in close formation still echoes over the bay every Tuesday and Wednesday morning when the team is home. The crowds still gather at the National Naval Aviation Museum viewing area, cameras pointed skyward.

How many more times they'll have that opportunity before a pause—if a pause comes—remains unclear. The Navy isn't saying. And Pensacola is left waiting.
